author: Abahlali_3
title: This August we honour the women of South Africa
content:
11 August 2026 Abahlali baseMjondolo Press Statement

This August we honour the women of South Africa

This August, in women’s month, we speak of the comrades who are mothers, daughters, sisters and grandmothers, comrades who wake up every morning in the shack settlements and carry the weight of a country that has forgotten them.

We honour the women who keep their families going under conditions of brutal impoverishment and the women who resist oppression. We honour the women in our movement.

But this is not a month of celebration.

No woman is fully free in South Africa. All women are at risk of violence. Impoverished women remain profoundly oppressed.

There is no celebration when women continue to live under very dangerous conditions.

There is no celebration when a woman must walk to a communal tap after dark and risk rape or attack.

There is no celebration when there is no electricity, no running water, no toilets, and no safety for children.

There is no celebration when a woman does not know if her home will be standing tomorrow because of evictions, fires, or political violence.

For millions of impoverished women in shacks, tin houses and backyards, every day is a fight for survival.

To celebrate while all this is true is to lie.

This August we honour all the women of our movement who refused to accept poverty as fate.

We honour Nqobile Nzuza who was murdered by a police officer on a road blockade in Cato Crest on 30 September 2013. She was seventeen years old and doing her matric. She joined the road blockade in protest against the brutal attacks on the Marikana Land Occupation in Cato Manor by the eThekwini Municipality. She was committed to the struggle for land.

We honour Comrade Thuli Ndlovu, a leader of Abahlali baseMjondolo in KwaNdengezi. She fought for land, for housing, and for the dignity of her community. She was assassinated on 27 September 2014 for confronting oppression.

We honour Comrade Nokuthula Mabaso, a leader of eKhenana Commune and of the Abahlali Women’s League. She was a mother, an organiser, and a builder of a community that fed itself and governed itself. She was assassinated on 5 May 2022 while her community was under attack. She knew that poor people must seize the right to land and to live with dignity.

Our brave comrades refused oppression and insisted on land and dignity. Thuli and Nokuthula were leaders.

We also honour other women who have given their lives in the struggle for justice.

Fikile Ntshangase was a leading member of the Mfolozi Community Environmental Justice Organisation (MCEJO) which opposed the destruction of people’s land and homes by coal mining. She was assassinated on 22 October 2020.

Babita Deokaran was an honest civil servant and a whistleblower in the Gauteng Department of Health. She exposed corruption and the theft of public money meant for the public hospitals and clinics that serve the poor. She was assassinated in 2021 for refusing to look away as powerful and dangerous men looted the healthcare system.

We have no interest in politicians who come with speeches and flowers and say nothing about the oppression we live today and nothing about our leaders who have given their lives in the struggle against this oppression.

1.⁠ ⁠Secure access to land and decent housing so no woman sleeps in fear of eviction or fire. 2.⁠ Access to basic services such as water, electricity, sanitation, and safe public lighting in every settlement. 3.⁠ ⁠An end to political killings and intimidation of women organisers. 4.⁠ ⁠An end to gender-based violence in homes, streets, schools and communities. 5.⁠ ⁠Decent work, healthcare and education so women are not forced to choose between feeding their children and their own health. 6. Reproductive healthcare and contraception available without humiliation or delay. 7. A livable guaranteed income in recognition of the unpaid care work that holds families and communities together. 8. Decisive action to reduce food prices on essential items. 9. An end to attempts to turn poor women against migrant and refugee women, since the enemy is landlessness, unemployment and state neglect, not our neighbours. 10.⁠ ⁠Accountability for the killings of Nqobile, Thuli, Nokuthula, Fikile, Babita and all the other murdered and assassinated women activists whose cases were closed and forgotten.

Poor women are not asking to be celebrated. We are demanding to be safe, to be housed, to be heard, to be alive.

Until that happens, August …

author: Hassan Alnaser, Kidus Lemma
title: Once bitter enemies Amhara, Tigray reach understandings in fight against Ethiopian govt
content:
In mid-August, the leader of the Amhara insurgency fighting to overthrow Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed made a surprising announcement. 


The collection of armed Amhara movements fighting in the country’s northwest under the unified Fano umbrella would join an alliance of seven other anti-government groups across the country, Fano leader Zemene Kassie

told

 the Swiss publication, Le Temps.

 


What makes the move surprising is that the alliance includes members of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), whom the Amhara forces that make up the Fano fought against during the 2020-2022 war.


In addition to the TPLF, the alliance includes forces from Gumuz, Oromo, the Berta people and Somalia, Zemene said. 


At the national level, the fight between Ethiopian oppositional groups and the government comes against the backdrop of a struggle over the future of the country’s multinational federal system and state’s right to self-determination. 


However, this tension has a larger regional dynamic given Ethiopia’s involvement in the war in Sudan and its expressed desire to secure access to the Red Sea either by diplomatic coup or by force. 


While fighting between the Fano and the Ethiopian government has transformed much of the Amhara Region into an active war zone since late 2023, the beginning of August saw clashes between TPLF forces and the Ethiopian military that threatened to transform long standing simmering tensions between the groups into an active war. 


An African Union diplomat based in Addis Ababa told

Mada Masr

 at the time that any expansion of the fighting in Tigray would have an impact on the calculations of every regional actor because the borders linking Sudan, Ethiopia and Eritrea are no longer merely dividing lines between states.

 They now form part of an interconnected regional security system in which domestic wars and geopolitical interests overlap, the diplomat added, making any new outbreak of fighting in Tigray a potential factor in reshaping the security landscape of the entire East African region.


The government has responded to the early August clashes with increased military activity. 


In a statement issued on Friday, the Tigray regional government

warned

the international community that the region is nearing “another catastrophic war.”

 


An economic and security blockade has escalated following clashes that broke out on August 1, the statement added, with air strikes and artillery shelling hitting civilian areas, causing casualties and destruction and disrupting cultural activities.


In an interview with Oromia Broadcasting Network on August 7, Abiy criticized the TPLF leadership, accusing it of clinging to outdated political methods and forging alliances that he said threaten stability. 


TPLF deputy chair Amanuel Assefa pointed to a strike on August 20, when a drone

hit

a residential area in Mekelle, Tigray’s capital.

 Residents speaking to Mada Masr confirmed the strike and said several homes were damaged.


Medical sources at Mekelle’s Ayder Specialized Hospital said 13 people were brought in with injuries following the strike, including five women and children, with three in serious condition. The injured ranged in age from two to 60, the sources said.


Tigrayan authorities also said a second strike hit near Mekelle University, though there is no confirmed information on casualties or damage as of the time of publishing.


The strike on Mekelle came only days after another attack that Tigrayan authorities attributed to the Ethiopian military, where a drone struck a farmers’ training center in the Dandera village, about 15 km from Mekelle, on August 18.


Site of drone strike in Mekelle, Tigray’s capital. August 20. Source: Tigray Communications Affairs Bureau via Facebook


While the government hit Tigray, Fano forces continued to secure strategic wins against the Ethiopian military. 


Fano forces in the Wollo provinces of Amhara – which borders southern Tigray — have

claimed

 significant military victories in the past week along the Raya and Ambasel fronts, capturing strategic cities, highway corridors and key positions beyond the Awash River.

 


Fano forces seized the cities of Robit and Aradum and moved within three km of the city of Kobo. Fano troops also took control of the main Waja-Kobo asphalt highway, a critical transit corridor leading to Addis Ababa. 


And on the Ambasel front, Fano forces ambushed government troops moving from Wuchale …

author: Krishna Kumar
title: 500,000 children are born with congenital heart disease in Africa. Where are the hospitals to treat them?
content:
When Tendai Moyo’s daughter, Rudorwashe Grace, was born in a Zimbabwean hospital, she struggled to breathe, her lips turned blue, and feeding exhausted her. Recognising instantly that her baby was seriously unwell, Tendai repeatedly sought medical help, but her concerns were ignored. Because her daughter’s illness was invisible and she appeared to others like a healthy baby, her symptoms were even dismissed as witchcraft.


Tendai Moyo


It took six months of fighting for Rudorwashe Grace to be diagnosed with tricuspid atresia and cardiomegaly, a severe congenital heart defect. By then, valuable time had been lost. For babies with the most serious heart defects, those months can be the difference between life and death.


But even after diagnosis, Tendai couldn’t find the care her baby needed. At the time, Zimbabwe had only one paediatric cardiologist for a population of 15 million, practising privately in Harare, about 400 kilometres away. With no hope that surgery could take place locally, Tendai’s only chance was to raise around US$20,000 to send her daughter to India for treatment.


Tragically, her daughter died at just 10 months old. Her death was not inevitable. It was the result of systemic delays, missed opportunities by governments and policymakers and a health system that was not equipped to respond to congenital heart disease.


What went wrong?


Tendai’s story is sadly far from unique. Congenital heart disease (CHD) is one of the most common birth defects in the world, affecting up to one in every 50 newborns. Across Africa, this means

500,000 babies are born each year

 with damaged hearts. Some will have small defects that can be monitored, but at least a third will need critical treatment in their first year of life. Without it,

up to 85% of children with the severest form of CHD will die

.


For thousands of African children effective treatment is a matter of life and death. Despite this, across much of Africa, the systems needed to diagnose and treat CHD are dangerously out of reach for most families.


Outlined in the World Heart Federation’s yearly

World Heart Report

, as

many as 90% of children

 in some regions of Africa, such as Somalia, Djibouti, Niger and Chad, live in “paediatric heart health deserts” – areas with no timely access to safe diagnosis or care for congenital heart disease. The very few paediatric cardiac surgery centres in Africa are often concentrated in capital cities, where the costs of travel and accommodation alone can render surgery unfeasible.


As the report illustrates, congenital heart disease often falls between categories, prompting planning and policy misalignments on a global scale. It is present at birth, but not always included in maternal and newborn health programmes. It is a heart condition, but often missing from cardiovascular disease plans, which are typically designed around adults and place emphasis on lifestyle factors and hypertension, rather than conditions present from birth. It requires surgery, but a very specialised surgery that may not be included in national surgical strategies.


Even when safe, affordable and timely surgery can take place, a decent quality of life can only be assured by lifelong follow-up care. In today’s global healthcare lottery, the result is that many children fall through the cracks.


Creating pathways


Despite the prevalence of these “heart-health deserts”, encouragingly, there are models from low- and middle-income regions that can be adapted. Kerala, in India, is widely lauded for its efforts to approach congenital heart disease as a population health challenge, rather than with a case-by-case treatment model. When Kerala channelled funding and resources into this approach, the state developed a “Continuum of Care” for CHD to not only encapsulate recognition, diagnosis and referral, but with provisions for transport, integrated collaboration with the private sector for surgical treatment and follow-up care.


The results of this shift in approach during the programme’s first six years

speak for themselves

: 22876 children with suspected CHD were registered; 767 newborns and 2612 infants (30 days-1 year) underwent a therapeutic procedure that typically involved open-heart surgery. Most newborns with CHD were identified through prenatal or neonatal screening. During this period the infant mortality of the state of Kerala declined from 12/1000 to 6/1000.


Top-down vs. bottom-up


Despite systemic failings at a …

author: Noziphiwo Sigwela
title: Public land for the public good: Tafelberg ruling puts Cape Town on notice
content:
On the 2

nd

 of July 2026, the Constitutional Court handed down an unanimous judgement that will reshape how we understand the right to housing in South Africa.


The Tafelberg judgment (

Adonisi v Minister for Transport and Public Works, Western Cape; Minister of Human Settlements v Minister for Transport and Public Works, Western Cape

 [2026] ZACC 29 (2 July 2026)

) declared the 2015 sale of the Tafelberg property at 353 Main Road, Sea Point, Cape Town, unlawful.


This ruling highlighted the failure by the Western Cape government and City of Cape Town to fulfil their constitutional duties to redress spatial injustice by providing affordable housing in well-located areas. This battle was championed by urban land movement,

Reclaim the City

, with support from NGO,

Ndifuna Ukwazi

. In a celebrated outcome, both levels of government were ordered to submit detailed reports to the high court within three months (2 October 2026).


But as we celebrate this victory, we must confront the sobering truth. This was only one of the City’s many failures. The same week the Constitutional Court affirmed the importance of spatial justice, the Public Protector released a devastating report on the City’s failure to provide basic municipal services to Langa Flats in Langa and in the township of Khayelitsha. The contrast could not be clearer. While the city and provincial governments fought for a decade to sell off prime public land in Sea Point, residents in Langa and Khayelitsha have been living without functioning sewers, fire safety equipment, clean water, and without the dignity that the constitution promises them.


Two cities, one constitution


The Public Protector’s report,

Systemic Investigation into Alleged Failure by the City of Cape Town to Provide Basic Municipal Services in Langa Flats and Khayelitsha Township

, reads like an indictment of a city that has forgotten half its residents.


In Langa Flats, sewer infrastructure has been in a state of disrepair for 14 years. Firehose reels and extinguishers that were promised to be repaired in March 2022 are still broken.


Residents have been forced to contribute R100 per household to hire cleaners for communal areas, a responsibility that rightfully belongs to the municipality. Housing units have cracked walls that, despite repeated commitments, are years later still to be assessed.


According to the report by the Public Protector, Town Two Clinic does not have smoke detectors or CCTV cameras. Earlier this year, the security company at the clinic fell victim to extortion rackets that are ravaging the community.


In Khayelitsha, the picture is no better. At SST-Marikana, residents who were relocated by the City to make way for sewer repairs were moved to a site without access to electricity or adequate water.


In multiple inspections of the area, the Public Protector found none of the 143 water taps that the City claimed to have provided. Relocated families relied on a self-connected communal tap – a pipe pressed down with a cement block, providing only a trickle of water.


An elderly wheelchair-bound resident was left alone without accessible water or electricity, in conditions “neither safe nor conducive to his health and wellbeing”.


At the

Matthew Goniwe

 and

Town Two

 clinics, there were no smoke detectors, and no functional CCTV cameras, with paper records stored in rooms without fire detection. Staff at

Matthew Goniwe

 reported that the clinic could go without electricity for two to three weeks at a time. This is not a failure of resources alone, but a failure of

priorities

.


The spatial logic of neglect


What connects Tafelberg to Langa and Khayelitsha is not just geography but a spatial logic that has persisted since Apartheid. Well-located land in Sea Point is fiercely protected for the wealthy, while poor and working-class communities are pushed to the urban periphery and are neglected there – out of sight, out of mind!


The Constitutional Court’s Tafelberg judgment recognised this explicitly. title: Warraq residents demonstrate to protest ‘state ignoring legitimate demands’
content:
Hundreds of Warraq Island residents held a protest march on Tuesday, after the head of the authority tasked with developing the island failed to respond to demands they submitted last week, one of the participants in the march told Mada Masr.


Hundreds of residents gathered in the street on Tuesday morning, on the deadline they had given authorities to respond to demands they submitted last week, including that they be granted lands within the state development project, according to the participant as well as videos published by other residents who attended the march.


The crowd then marched toward the New Warraq City Development headquarters, where a heavy security deployment awaited them. Security officials told them that the head of the authority asked for a small group to enter for negotiations. 


The protestors refused, instead demanding that the authority’s head come down to meet them, in an attempt to get a direct response to the demands they had already submitted in writing.


The resident who took part in Tuesday’s march said the authority head’s refusal to come down and meet the residents sparked anger among many of them, but that they kept it in check out of their keenness to keep the protest peaceful. 


But it showed “a lack of consideration, especially since he didn’t meet us when we came to hand over the demands,” the resident said.


The same sentiment was clear at the protest. “Nobody has paid us any attention,” one of the protesters

called

 out to the assembled crowd. “At this moment, we register our objection to the state’s disregard for our legitimate and just demands by saying just one thing: God is sufficient for us, and he is the best disposer of all affairs,” indicating the group’s loss of faith in the authorities’ seriousness. 


The residents then continued their peaceful protest march along the route that had been agreed to in advance. While the march had been planned without chants, still, the residents raised similar cries of “God is sufficient for us” and “one hand.”


At the end of the march, the residents agreed to meet again on Friday to discuss their next steps, and raised the possibility of disrupting ongoing development work on the island.


The residents had submitted a list of demands to the authority on August 18, foremost among them that they be allocated a plot of land within the island’s redevelopment area, where residents who have chosen to stay could build their own homes, according to a defined timeline, with clear and specific implementation mechanisms and fair conditions. They also put forward other demands concerning living and security conditions on the island.


The group handed their written demands to the authority’s deputy chair at the time, with the head elsewhere with another group of Warraq residents, inspecting one of the island’s schools, supposedly to assess potential upgrades.


The resident described to Mada Masr the authority head’s meeting with that group as part of security attempts to “divide.”


One of the people in the group that did not join Tuesday’s march said there were some who had not attended the recent meeting that produced the list of demands. The group who went with the authority head on his school visit opposes holding marches to the authority’s offices, they told Mada Masr. Instead, they have been trying to communicate with officials at the authority and pressure them to implement “as many things as possible that would allow us to keep living on the island,” they continued, adding that they are convinced the government would not agree to give residents land on the island to replace their homes.


The source pointed to what they saw as officials responding to some of the residents’ service-related demands, including bringing back sewage pumping trucks and beginning to clear demolition waste that had piled up along the island’s roads.


Those same measures were described by the resident who took part in Tuesday’s march as “painkillers that don’t work anymore.”


“Some people come and tell you, ‘We brought services,’ when they are our rights that were taken away from us in the first place,” they said. “They’re moving to get the land, so I’m demanding the land.” 


The island has seen a spike in

tensions and incidents between residents and security forces

 in recent weeks, as residents face restrictions on the delivery of construction and building materials.

author: The Canadian Press
title: ‘Then, now and always’: Carney says it will always be Lake Ontario after Trump order
content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canadians know Lake Ontario will always be known by its original name, after U.S. President Donald Trump on Thursday signed an executive order to change it to Lake America.


In a post on social media, Carney said “we know that America is changing.”


“Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms,” Carney posted. “Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always.”


“The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big,'” Carney added.


“The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America.”


Tensions between the two countries have escalated since trade negotiations fell apart on Friday. Both countries have accused each other of implementing eleventh-hour changes.


Carney has said the agreement became untenable. The federal government unveiled its retaliatory measures, set to go in place next month, on Tuesday.


The relationship between Canada and the United States was already rocky before recent negotiations. Trump’s tariffs and threats of annexation have angered and confused the historically close ally.


Trump first threatened to rename the body of water during an escalating war of words with Ontario Premier Doug Ford earlier this week.


The two exchanged insults, with Ford calling the president a bully, among other things, and Trump saying the premier was a “less charismatic, intelligent” version of his late brother, Rob.


Sitting near a map with the name “Lake America” over the body of water on Thursday in the Oval Office, Trump said Canada has been difficult to deal with and repeated claims the country was ripping off the United States.


“They want to be treated like a state but they are not a state,” Trump said.


When asked why he was targeting American allies with these types of actions instead of American adversaries, Trump said “they haven’t treated us well.”


“The Canadian officials have treated us very badly,” Trump said. “They are nasty people.”


Ford said on social media Thursday that “it’s Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever.”


Interior Secretary Doug Burgum — who previously was governor of border state North Dakota — posted on social media “the places and waters that border our nation and support our economy should reflect the greatness of the United States.” U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra shared Burgum’s post.


But the renaming was quickly condemned as a distraction by others.


Republican Gov. Phil Scott of Vermont called the move disappointing. In a post on social media he said “we should be at the negotiating table, finding a path forward that strengthens both the U.S. and Canadian economies.”


“Further escalating tensions does nothing to help American or Canadian families and businesses,” Scott said.


Democrat Gov. Janet Mills of Maine posted a tip for the president on social media: “focus on lowering costs for your constituents instead of doodling on maps.”


In Canada, the move prompted incredulity, with Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston posting on social media that “we’re into some real foolishness now.”


“It’s Lake Ontario, buddy,” Houston said.


At an unrelated news conference in Winnipeg, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew described the situation as an over-the-hill rock star playing old hits at a casino.


“I think that’s the part of Donald Trump’s presidency we’re at now,” Kinew said. “Like he thought he had a real hit, a real golden oldie with the Gulf of Mexico, and he’s trying to bring back that, and he’s trying to play the hits for his base. But I think everybody here thinks it’s a little sad and it’s not his best work.”


Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said no executive order will change the lake’s name and “it doesn’t belong to President Donald Trump to rename on a whim.” He said Canada should not respond to stunts and distractions and stay focused on what the country can control.


Lake Ontario — one of the five Great Lakes — is located between Ontario and New York. The Canadian province is named after the lake.


The White House did not respond to questions about whether any Indigenous groups in the United States were consulted before the name change.


Trump pointed to his decision in 2025 to sign an executive order changing the name …

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Jury Finds DeSantis Admin Diverted $10M Marked for Poor Children to GOP Coffers
content:
The funds were given to Florida from a settlement with a company that was overcharging Medicaid for prescription drugs.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

A Florida grand jury has found that Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis’s administration misappropriated millions of dollars in taxpayer funds that were marked to help children get health insurance but instead went to right-wing political groups and the state Republican Party.

The grand jury found that state officials funneled $10 million in funding from a Medicaid-related settlement to the Hope Florida Foundation, a faith-based organization which was supposed to use the funding to help poor children with health coverage, according to reporting by CBS Miami.

But the charity, founded by DeSantis’s wife, quickly funnelled half of the money to the right-wing group Secure Florida’s Future, and the other half to Save Our Society From Drugs in 2024. The funding was ultimately used to help defeat a citizen’s ballot measure, Amendment 3, which would have legalized recreational marijuana in the state.

The grand jury concluded that there is not sufficient evidence to charge anyone criminally because “nobody will take responsibility” for the decision to send the money to Hope Florida or “had any memory of who made it.”

The money originated from a multi-state settlement with for-profit health care company Centene, which agreed to pay a $1 billion settlement in 2021 for allegedly overcharging numerous state Medicaid programs for prescription drugs. As many other states settled their cases, DeSantis’s administration ignored Centene’s request to resolve the matter, reports said, but finally agreed to accept the $67 million in 2024. The state decided that $57 million would be returned to taxpayers while the rest would go to Hope Florida, apparently bypassing the state legislature to make that decision.

The decision to give the money to Hope Florida was already highly controversial at the time, with detractors noting that it was DeSantis’s wife’s charity.

But the grand jury said they were told Hope Florida was chosen as a recipient because it “was compensation for ripping off sick poor children and Hope Florida’s mission and work aligned with the purpose of serving needy children with health issues.” In reality, the charity’s operations were a black box, and any plausible reasoning for the decision “was rendered moot by the fact that the money only stayed in Hope Florida’s account for a couple of days.”

DeSantis said on Thursday that the grand jury’s findings were a “lie” and that whoever leaked a copy of the report committed a “crime.” The day before, he said that he “wasn’t involved in the settlement agreement, but I’m very happy with how everything was done.”

News of the findings comes as the Trump administration has whipped up a frenzy about supposed fraud with regard to states’ disbursements of Medicaid — a campaign that the administration then used to withhold funding from Medicaid funds from the Democratically-controlled states of California and Minnesota.

author: Daron Letts
title: Iqaluit youth are throwing rocks at taxis — again
content:
Rocks hurled by young people in Iqaluit have caused an estimated $6,000 in damages to Caribou Cab’s fleet since June 21, said CEO Danny Savard in a letter to city council on Tuesday.


“It may only be a matter of time before someone is hurt,” he wrote.


The company, which maintains more than 80 vehicles, has reported nine instances of rocks thrown at their taxis to the city in the past two months.


“Our intention is not to blame, but rather to bring awareness to the seriousness of what is happening and work together on a solution,” Savard said.


While no drivers have been physically injured, the experience is unnerving, said

Yannick Levesque, Caribou Cab’s nighttime supervisor, Thursday in an email.


“These events can cause mental trauma,” Levesque said. “Drivers get rocks thrown every night on their cabs.”


Levesque added that taxi drivers aren’t the only victims — regular vehicles are targeted as well.


He suggested a 10 p.m. curfew for youth could help.


Rock throwing is a recurring issue in Iqaluit.


Caribou Cab’s self-employed drivers

staged a protest

 in September 2021, parking their vehicles over what they perceived as a lack of response to the issue.


The walkout caused bars and other businesses to temporarily shut down. Rock-throwing

continued

 in subsequent years, however.


Half of the cab company’s drivers are owner-operators of their own vehicles.


Prime One Taxi also operates six cabs in the city. Drivers there have also experienced vandalism in the past, said driver Sam Naas.


“Someone broke my windshield at NorthMart last November,” he said.


Naas did not see who threw the rock.


“I wish I knew,” he said.


RCMP has investigated nine occurrences reported since June 1, said spokesperson Cpl. Ashley Daley, in an email on Thursday.


Daley declined to reveal the outcome of the investigations but did say police have increased “proactive” patrols both in the day and night.


Engagement by the RCMP and city officials helped curb the issue in the past, said Savard.


“We want to work collaboratively with local authorities and the community rather than simply react after another vehicle is damaged or, worse, after someone is injured,” he said.


City of Iqaluit spokesperson Geoff Byrne declined to comment on this story.

author: Kelsie kilawna
title: As syilx families reel from wildfire losses, designers launch community fundraiser
content:
Michael Conlin (left) and Brian Caron, co-owners of the Nation Party Collective, wear

a wildfire-relief shirt they created

 to support Okanagan Indian Band families affected by the Bradley Creek wildfire.

Photo by kelsie marchand (kilawna)


When a wildfire moved through nk̓maplqs — the head of Okanagan Lake — earlier this month, the images that flooded social media were predictable: orange skies, flames, billowing smoke, and devastation.


But while the Bradley Creek fire’s

destruction was real

, many of the images circulating online were not. 


Some were from other fires; several were entirely fake — generated by artificial intelligence. 


“People are always trying to take advantage of tragedies that happen in our community,” says Michael Conlin, an Okanagan Indian Band (OKIB) member who co-founded Nation Party Collective with Brian Caron. 


“It’s like a slap in the face to the people that are actually going through this.”


Brian, who is Métis, agreed the AI-generated images circulating widely online felt exploitative — and completely detached from the reality of what was unfolding

on the ground

 within OKIB.


“It kind of grossed me out,” says Brian.


“I understand we want to raise awareness, but do we really need somebody AI-generating a whole community that’s actually on fire?”


Since the fire quickly moved through the First Nation of nearly 2,600 residents, OKIB has been in recovery mode. 


A formal damage assessment by Canada Task Force 1 found 245 structures damaged or destroyed.


As of August 26, the

fire

 was still burning at 26 square kilometres in size, but classified as “under control,” with crews still working to extinguish and patrol the blaze. 


OKIB Chief Dan Wilson said his community is “in the process of recovery” and that it’s “going to take a while,” he shared on the community’s social media.


As the community and its leaders depended on social media to share essential information, Michael and Brian had noticed the AI-generated images circulating online. 


They knew they had to do something different —

a design

 that accurately reflects the beauty and the ongoing strength of the syilx Okanagan people.


OKIB member Michael Conlin says

Nation Party Collective’s fundraiser

 is one ‘small way we can give something back’ to his community after a devastating wildfire earlier this month.

Photo by kelsie marchand (kilawna)


Collaboration rooted in community


Business partners Michael and Brian started

their clothing company

 about a year-and-a-half ago. 


Its name came from a street in “Prince George” where they used to record music: Nation Crescent. The company has grown quickly. 


“We started off rapping,” Michael says. 


“And then my partner went to graphic design school, and I was like, ‘Let’s just create a clothing company.'”


The pair had just returned from Back to Batoche Days, the largest outdoor Indigenous festival in “Canada,” held each July at the historic site of the 1885 Battle of Batoche in Saskatchewan.


The four-day celebration of Métis culture draws tens of thousands of visitors each year for fiddling, jigging, traditional foods, and live music.


“That was our big goal,” Brian says of attending the festival. 


“We got there like three, four years ahead of schedule.”


They had just come from Batoche. Michael left right away to perform in Tkaronto (Toronto), and then the fire hit. His family evacuated while he was on-stage, across the continent. 


Brian was back in the Okanagan, watching the smoke climb. Both wanted to help, but neither knew where to start.


“I have a newborn, I do graphic design, and I’m full-time in construction,” Brian says. 


“The only way I could really help is something like this.”


‘If we don’t do it, somebody else will’


When Brian reached out to Michael, AI-generated wildfire images were already popping up across social media. Michael contacted his relative David Wilson,

a syilx artist

 who is respected as a painter and Knowledge Keeper. 


“This is a good moment to collaborate,” Brian recalls thinking, “and get something out there that’s going to help people.”


David was already immersed in multiple projects — including carving 13 canoes — and gave Brian access to his catalog of artwork.


Brian, a graphic designer, digitized elements from David’s paintings, including pictographs from a piece featuring the Spirit of the syilx, and adapted them for the shirt.

author: Giovanna DeStefanis
title: Women’s Equality Day: Many Gains, Still Work To Do
content:
On August 26, 1920, the 19th Amendment was certified, prohibiting the denial of the right to vote on the basis of sex. More than a century later, Women’s Equality Day commemorates that historic victory and the generations of suffragists who fought to secure it.

Women have won extraordinary gains in the 106 years since the 19th Amendment. But the right to vote was only one of the many rights women fought to secure. For much of US history, women were systematically excluded from political decision-making, denied equal access to education and employment, and treated as legally and economically dependent on men.

Through decades of organizing, litigation, and political action, feminists helped expand women’s access to education and the workplace, challenged sex discrimination, fought for protections against sexual harassment, and won greater economic independence, including the ability to obtain credit in their own names. Feminists also fought for access to contraception and abortion, recognizing that the ability to decide whether and when to have children is fundamental to women’s equality and autonomy.

Those struggles transformed the lives of generations of women. Today, women are outpacing men in college completion across every major racial and ethnic group in the US, while women are running for public office in record numbers. From the ballot box to the classroom, the workplace to the legislature, these gains did not happen by accident. They were won by generations of feminists who refused to accept inequality as inevitable. Even as women continue to break barriers and make historic progress, those hard-won gains are not guaranteed.

Yet Women’s Equality Day does not mean that women have achieved equality.

“I never thought that in the US we’d have people arguing to go back to the 19th century,” said Feminist Majority Foundation President and co-founder Eleanor Smeal. “It’s the 21st.”

Today, hard-won rights are once again under attack. The right to make decisions about our own bodies has been stripped away from millions of women since the Supreme Court overturned Roe. Across the country, abortion bans are forcing women to continue pregnancies against their will, while attacks on contraception and other reproductive health care threaten to further limit women’s control over their own lives. Taking that decision away is an attempt to take that power away as well.

Even the rights commemorated by Women’s Equality Day are being questioned. Some have openly advocated for restricting women’s voting for “household voting” that could give husbands greater control over how families vote. The fact that taking away women’s independent voting power is being discussed at all is a reminder that hard-won rights cannot be taken for granted.

“We never thought bad things would happen again,” said Kathy Spillar, executive director of Feminist Majority Foundation. “We demand equality, no less—but we must ensure that there is equality.”

That fight includes securing the Equal Right Amendment to explicitly prohibit discrimination on the basis of sex in the Constitution. Although the ERA has been fully ratified by the required 38 states, it has yet to be recognized as part of the Constitution. The majority of states have also adopted some form of constitutional protection for equal rights based on sex—or State ERA’s—but protections vary across the country.

Women’s Equality Day should be a celebration of how far women have come, but not a declaration of victory. We can celebrate the suffragists who fought for the ballot, the feminists who expanded women’s access to education and economic independence, and the generations of women who broke barriers in politics and public life. But equality is not guaranteed. We must continue fighting for reproductive freedom, an end to violence against women, equal opportunity and representation, and constitutional equality. Women’s Equality Day is a reminder of what feminists have won, and why we must keep fighting to protect it.

title: Enbridge Line 5 Spills Natural Gas Liquids in Northern Wisconsin
content:
Saxon, WI — Enbridge’s aging

Line 5

 pipeline is spilling natural gas liquids in northern Wisconsin. The rupture occurred just east of the Bad River Reservation near Lake Superior on August 25, 2026. According to Enbridge, an unoccupied semi truck rolled into an excavation site and struck the pipeline.


The Canadian oil giant faces numerous legal challenges over its operation of Line 5. The 73-year-old pipeline carries oil and natural gas liquids through the heart of the Great Lakes region. Experts warn that it risks rupturing into the world’s largest bodies of freshwater.


Enbridge’s Line 5 pipeline

, originally routed across

Bad River Band

 tribal land under easements

dating to 1953

, is now being rerouted along a new 41.1-mile corridor through

1854 Treaty Territory

 in Ashland County, Wis., crossing 186 waterways, 612 acres of wetlands, and hard bedrock across the

Penokee-Gogebic Range

, the zone of greatest geological uncertainty along the route.


Line 5 alone has had roughly 30 on-land releases, totaling around one million gallons of oil.

See our report from May for more information

.

title: L’importanza di Elinor Ostrom per Tutti Noi
content:
Di

Keith Taylor

. Originale:

What Elinor Ostro

m Means For All Of Us

, del 21 giugno 2012. Tradotto da

Enrico Sanna

.


Mi ha addolorato apprendere che una delle mie principali ispiratrici, la professoressa Elinor Ostrom, è morta di cancro al pancreas lo scorso martedì dodici giugno. La sua opera fa parte della mia crescita sia come accademico che come essere umano. Quando ero studente di dottorato presso il dipartimento dello sviluppo umano e comunitario dell’Università dell’Illinois, l’opera della Ostrom ha fatto da base alla mia passione per le associazioni cooperative viste come contropotere o come correttivo del corrosivo sistema di dipendenza.


Nel dispiacere, la grande soddisfazione è sapere che la Ostrom ci ha lasciato un compito da portare avanti: interi archivi e opere di ricerca, cinquant’anni passati a indirizzare giovani studenti verso la ricerca di soluzioni; e poi approcci innovativi alla comprensione del comportamento umano tramite la creazione, presso l’Università dell’Indiana, di un istituto di ricerca chiamato affettuosamente “Laboratorio Ostrom”. Se molti parlano del personaggio, e non c’è dubbio che questo è un attributo fortemente positivo della sua eredità, io preferisco concentrarmi su come la Ostrom ci ha aiutato a capire come possiamo governare noi stessi, una questione di fondo che accomuna singolarmente gli esperimenti americano e anarchico. Ma vorrei anche concentrarmi sul nostro dovere di dare vita alle conoscenze frutto della dura ricerca della Ostrom.


La Ostrom era un accademico sui generis. Trascendeva il dibattito di gran parte delle cerchie marxiste dogmatiche, libertarie e economiche eterodosse sconvolgendo le divisioni ideologiche, sapeva che interrogativi complessi richiedevano risposte complesse perché hanno grosse implicazioni sociali e economiche:


• Le persone sono spinte da considerazioni diverse dal crudo egoismo?


• Le persone sono sempre in lotta per il potere e il controllo?


• Le persone sono in grado di superare le grandi barriere per affrontare questioni critiche come il cambiamento climatico?


La Ostrom (e suo marito Vincent che le sopravvive e che è un importante teorico degli ordini istituzionali policentrici) ha studiato queste questioni cercando di capire com’è che le persone di fronte a dilemmi sociali utilizzano la “scienza e l’arte dell’associazione”. Gli studi della Ostrom dimostrano che l’uomo ha la capacità di sviluppare soluzioni in comune per poi agire in concerto e evitare i problemi.


Senza il lavoro pionieristico della Ostrom, saremmo probabilmente ancora impantanati in vecchi dibattiti sull’egemonia, sull’opposizione pubblico privato o sull’efficacia della conoscenza di esperti rispetto alla conoscenza locale. La Ostrom ci lascia l’aspirazione ad un bene più grande per le persone; persone che hanno la capacità di gestire i propri affari collaborando tra loro per un futuro migliore. Grazie al suo pensiero, abbiamo la possibilità di non dover più sfidare le politiche basate sull’autorità di pochi: ci rafforza il fatto di sapere che “i tanti” hanno un’enorme capacità di controllare il proprio destino.


Io stesso, in qualità di docente ospite, ho l’onore di dar vita, presso l’Università dell’Indiana, al Vincent and Elinor Ostrom Workshop in materia di politologia e analisi politica. Si tratta, sulla tradizione degli Ostrom, di far leva sulle teorie sul policentrismo, il governo democratico e le economie pubbliche locali, al fine di capire meglio il cooperativismo negli Stati Uniti. Si parte dall’intuizione ostromiana per cui la società non si limita allo stato o il mercato ma è un ricco intreccio di istituzioni ritagliate su misura dei bisogni di chi dipende da esse, istituzioni la cui forma ha un suo peso sulla comunità che le ospita. Io credo che le cooperative possano aiutare a correggere l’attuale scadimento della società, ma solo la ricerca può confermarlo. Fortunatamente, l’Ostrom Workshop offre preziosi strumenti che ci guideranno nella ricerca di queste verità.


Pur non avendo mai avuto, purtroppo, la possibilità di lavorare con una persona così importante, mi è capitato di incontrare la Ostrom in due occasioni e di lavorare con un centro di ricerca ispirato alle sue brillanti idee.


Dall’operato della Ostrom traspare un profondo interesse per il futuro dell’uomo e una fiducia ottimistica nella nostra capacità di risolvere i problemi di tutti. La sua opera ha fortunatamente fornito a noi le indicazioni su come acquisire quella …

title: Shaken Baby Syndrome Has Been Largely Debunked. Courts Are Still Catching Up.
content:
This story was co-published with


Truthout

.


  By the time Mason Tucker Smith was 2 years old, his mother, Mary Katherine Smith, had taken him to the doctor dozens of times.


  Tucker had frequent ear infections, high fevers, and episodes of vomiting. On at least six occasions, he had seizures, but the doctors repeatedly reassured his mother, who goes by Katie, that these were benign “breath-holding spells” that would resolve on their own.


  On the day of his collapse, July 30, 2014, Tucker had another seizure while Katie’s housemate, Jeremy Kitchens, was watching him in their bedroom and Katie was making dinner, according to her statement to the police.


  As she approached the bedroom door, she heard a “thud.” Katie entered the room and Kitchens told her that Tucker was having another “episode.” Katie told police that she found Tucker unconscious on the ground. Believing that this was another breath-holding episode, she picked him up and put him on the bed. She left him in Kitchens’s care while she drove her daughter to meet a friend. While she was gone, Tucker vomited.


  She returned to the house about 20 minutes later and checked Tucker’s oxygen level. When it began to drop, she called 911 and attempted to resuscitate him.


  At the hospital, a physician concluded Tucker had been shaken. He was declared dead on August 2 and Katie was charged with his murder.


  Two years later, Katie went to trial in Richmond County, Georgia, and was found guilty. The judge sentenced her to life in prison.


  Shaken baby syndrome (SBS), also known as abusive head trauma (AHT), has been largely debunked, with one New Jersey judge

calling it

 “akin to ‘junk science.’” While some courts have started to take a more critical look at SBS/AHT cases,

prosecutions have continued

 and

many people

 are still fighting their convictions.


The Appeal in Your Inbox


Subscribe to our newsletters for regular updates, analysis and context straight to your email.


Sign Up


  The so-called

triad of symptoms

 associated with SBS/AHT — bleeding around the eyes, bleeding between the skull and brain, and brain swelling —

can be caused by

 strokes, short-distance falls, seizures, and disease, among other things.


  Katie’s attorneys with the Southern Center for Human Rights say their investigation has revealed that she was convicted of a crime that never occurred.


  Experts retained by her legal team — a neurologist and a forensic pathologist — have concluded that Tucker died of undiagnosed epilepsy, which was caused by an undetected arteriovenous malformation (AVM) in his brain. AVM is a life-threatening condition that typically develops in utero, in which a person has abnormally tangled blood vessels that disrupt blood flow, deprive tissue of oxygen, and face risk of rupture.


  Forty-four people have been exonerated in SBS/AHT cases, according to the

National Registry of Exonerations

.


  Katie’s attorneys have filed a motion for a new trial and, on August 24, they will present their new evidence before the Superior Court of Richmond County.. The Augusta District Attorney’s Office is opposing Katie’s petition. The office did not respond to emails or calls seeking comment.


  “Tucker’s death was a tragedy, not a crime,” Katie’s lawyers wrote in their motion. “Tucker was sick from birth, and was living with an undiagnosed and untreated deadly brain condition.”


Tucker’s Medical Records


Truthout

reviewed Tucker’s medical records, which total about 278 pages. They reveal that Katie took him to the pediatrician more than 25 times, in addition to visits to specialists and the emergency room.


  The physicians reassured Katie that Tucker was a healthy child. They told her that when he became upset he held his breath until he passed out, but that this was nothing to be concerned about.


  Tucker’s first witnessed seizure occurred at daycare when he was five months old. Katie picked him up from daycare and took him to the pediatrician.


  “Patient was reported to have had eyes roll back and lose consciousness while eating baby food in a highchair (sort of slumped),” the doctor wrote.


  The pediatrician sent him to the hospital for an overnight observation. During the observation, Tucker “ate and slept well,” according to the medical records. Katie told the doctor that Tucker’s father, who had died shortly after Tucker’s death, and nephew each had experienced one seizure. The report does not recommend any further …

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Advocacy group travelling around James Bay to raise awareness of Ring of Fire
content:
A family from Northern Ontario is documenting a remote bay to raise awareness of what large-scale mining would do to the area and its biodiversity.


Jeronimo Kataquapit, a 21-year-old from Attawapiskat First Nation, is the founder of

Here We Stand

, a grassroots youth advocacy group which focuses on treaty rights and the environment south of the Hudson Bay.


On Aug. 21, Kataquapit announced that he and his parents and cousin, along with the family’s Labrador Retriever, Gunner, had kicked off a lengthy journey into James Bay, a remote, 68,300-square-kilometre section of the south bank of the Hudson Bay, near where Attawapiskat First Nation is located.


The journey, which was meant to document and broadcast the land and its several rivers to a social media audience, was done in direct response to the ongoing development of a road network to allow for mining in Ontario’s Ring of Fire.


“You can call this place many things, from the peatlands to the breathing lands, to the last frontier, or a sanctuary for all the biodiversity that calls this place home, but one thing I know it is for certain, is that it’s home,” Kataquapit said, in an update posted to social media.


“For me, I could stand here all day long, telling you all the reasons why we need to protect a place like this, but the first and only reason I need to protect this place, is because it’s home, and it’s who I am, and it’s where I belong,” he continued. “It will continue to be who I am and what I protect in the future.”


Gunner watches his owners boat toward the Ekwan River. Photo: Jeronimo Kataquapit/Facebook.


The Ring of Fire is a mineral-rich area of the bay, approximately 5,000-square-kilometres in size. According to the Government of Ontario, it contains “one of the most promising mineral development opportunities in the world.”


A few days after Kataquapit’s journey began, on Monday, Aug. 24,

Ontario announced

 the ground-breaking of a 107-kilometre, all-season road into the area.


Currently, the Ring of Fire is only accessible by air or winter ice roads for a “brief window” each year, according to the province.


The gravel road, proposed by Webequie First Nation, would allow for longer and simpler access to the natural resources there, which, according to Ontario, will “help unlock the vast economic potential of critical minerals in the region.”


Thus, the province stated, would “add $22 billion to Ontario’s economy, create 70,000 good-paying jobs, strengthen domestic supply chains and support long-term economic growth and prosperity for First Nations communities and northern Ontario.”


Alongside Webequie, the road is also being built in collaboration with Aroland and Marten Falls First Nations, which signed community partnership agreements in October and November 2025, respectively.


However, several other First Nations are speaking out about the environmental detriment this would have on the area.


A map of the Ring of Fire in northern Ontario.


APTN News

recently reported

 that on July 23, advocacy group

Friends of the Attawapiskat River

 filed a request for a judicial review of the project, saying that Ottawa’s own

federal impact assessment

 found that the road would cause “significant” damage to the environment and Indigenous rights.


“Where I call home, is one of the last remaining pristine, intact, and vast ecosystems left on the planet,” Kataquapit stated, in the journey’s announcement. “They are called the peatlands and are known to us as the breathing lands of Mother Earth. They store billions upon billions of tons of carbon and sequester millions of tons each year.


“I want people to see that what happens here, in the peatlands where the Ring of Fire is proposed, is inherently connected to the life of the Bay, our life, our health.”


Here We Stand has also spoken out against Bill 5, the

Protect Ontario by Unleashing our Economy Act

, and Bill C-5, the

One Canadian Economy Act

,

 which were both passed in June 2025.


Bill 5

 allows for Ontario to create ‘special economic zones,’ which, according to legislation, means the provincial government has the authority to exempt large-scale projects being built in these zones from regulations under other bills such as the

Ontario Heritage Act

 and the E

nvironmental Assessment Act

, among others.


According to

Chiefs of Ontario

, the bill “significantly weakens environmental protections, reduces oversight of mining and development projects, and limits …

author: Chris Walker
title: Trump Signs Executive Order Renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America”
content:
The president also indicated he may try to “rename” either the Pacific or Atlantic oceans — or, possibly both of them.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Amid an ongoing trade war with Canada, President Donald Trump issued an executive order on Thursday renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” despite the fact that a majority of its surface area resides within Canadian territory.

Trump’s executive order did not discuss the breakdown of trade negotiations. Instead, the order, titled “Honoring the American History of the Great Lakes and Renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America,” claimed the president was changing the lake’s name to “to recognize the extraordinary contributions of the American people and the rich heritage of our history by naming great natural landmarks for our shared achievements.”

The order also stated that the U.S. is the “greatest protector of the Great Lakes, including the body of water currently known as Lake Ontario” — despite Trump administration policies that threaten the safety and cleanliness of the lakes.

The order requires the Interior Department to “rename as ‘Lake America’ the body of water currently named as Lake Ontario” in all official map-related government documents, “including on executive department and agency maps, contracts, and other documents and communications.” Although social media posts from the administration after Trump signed the order indicated it would become “effective immediately,” the department’s actions may take up to a calendar month to complete.

EFFECTIVE IMMEDIATELY: Lake Ontario is renamed to LAKE AMERICA! 🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/ZFww8PexiW

The change only affects government maps in the U.S. As an international body of water, Canada is not compelled to change the name of the lake, and is likely to continue calling it Lake Ontario. Other countries could decide whether to recognize the name change.

Trump also indicated he may not be done renaming large bodies of water, and indicated that he may look at “changing” the names of oceans next.

“If you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake,” Trump said during the signing ceremony, referring also to his changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America” in U.S. documents. “Now, all we need is an ocean. So maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them.”

Trump says he might change the names of the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans next pic.twitter.com/460MysiWKa

The name change could affect more than just relations with Canada. Like the Gulf, Trump could try to punish entities that kept the old name intact — including news organizations — as the White House sought to restrict the press credentials of The Associated Press after it wouldn’t change its style guide last year.

“This is stupid bullshit but extremely pernicious stupid bullshit that reporters and news outlets can be penalized for failing to respect,” Matthew Gertz, senior fellow at Media Matters for America, said in a post on Bluesky.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), whose home state borders Canada, also criticized the action as a distraction from real issues Americans are worried about.

“The American people don’t want to rename Lake Ontario Lake America. They want affordable healthcare, childcare, housing, education & nutrition assistance — all of which you have massively cut in order to pay for your $1 trillion tax break to the top 1%,” Sanders wrote on X, directing his post toward Trump himself.

As Trump toyed with the idea last week, Chief Margaret Sault of the Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation condemned the proposed change, noting that the name preceded the arrival of European colonizers to the continent.

“Lake Ontario has existed for thousands of years, long before Canada and the United States became the countries we know today. … You can change a label on a map, but you cannot change the relationship that our people have with these lands and waters,” Sault said. “You cannot rename away our history.”

author: CMI Argentina
title: Rosario: movilización contra los femicidios y en reclamo de la emergencia en violencia de género
content:
Las organizaciones decidieron movilizarse luego de que se conocieran tres femicidios en 15 días.


Foto: Aire Libre- Rosario


Escuchar el reporte de Darío Uliassi desde Aire Libre Radio Comunitaria.


Concentraron este miércoles a las 17 frente a la Municipalidad de Rosario y finalizaron con un acto en la puerta de la sede de Gobernación de la provincia en la ciudad.


De la movilización participaron organizaciones feministas, sociales y políticas que se expresaron en contra de la violencia machista y reclamaron justicia por los femicidios.


En la provincia de Santa Fe se registraron más de 30 femicidios en lo que va del año. Además, se contabilizaron 10 víctimas más que en el mismo período del año pasado.


“Paren de matarnos” fue la consigna que encabezó la movilización donde las organizaciones advirtieron por la suba de casos, que se profundizan con el desmantelamiento de las políticas de género en los distintos niveles del Estado.


En declaraciones a Aire Libre, Gabriela Sosa, referente del movimiento feminista Mujeres por la Matria Latinoamericana (Mumalá), exigió la sanción de una ley provincial que declare la emergencia en violencia de género y que se cumpla la ordenanza local que declaró la emergencia hace un tiempo.


“Hemos presentado proyectos para que se declare la emergencia en violencia de género en Santa Fe y también que se pueda aplicar aquella ordenanza de hace varios años que ya declaraba la emergencia en Rosario y que disponía de recursos que siguen estando pendientes”.


Foto: Aire Libre- Rosario


Sosa también denunció las consecuencias del desmantelamiento de políticas públicas: “Esta quita de recursos, a la par de los discursos de odios, comienzan a impactar que las mujeres cada vez denunciamos menos, un 9% de la víctimas habían denunciado a su agresor anteriormente”.


Y agregó: “Por supuesto faltan campañas de prevención, faltan que los medios de comunicación tengan pautas de los estados municipales, provinciales y nacionales para informar de qué hacer”.

author: Nahuel Lag
title: Nêgo Bispo y el confluir del mundo quilombola
content:
Por Antônio Bispo dos Santos*


Desde los inicios de mi vida, mis ancestros me orientaron para escuchar los cantos de los pájaros y los chirridos del bosque. Entiendo el ambiente donde di mis primeros pasos como una de las plataformas de lanzamiento de mi trayectoria. Un recuerdo maravilloso de aquel tiempo, que todavía pulsa, es despertar oyendo el canto de la bandada informando las condiciones meteorológicas del día.


Los pájaros nos avisaban si iba a llover, si iba a salir el sol o si iba a estar nublado. Informado, entonces, incluso antes de levantarme, ya tenía noción de cómo sería el día. Otro latido de los recuerdos de infancia es el camino del campo que hacíamos junto con los mayores, la generación de mamá y la generación de la abuela. Oíamos los sonidos emitidos por el bosque, a partir del movimiento del viento y las aguas de los arroyos, ríos y cascadas, dependiendo de por donde pasábamos.


En el camino al campo, los pájaros continuaban con sus cantos, celebrando la abundancia que habían encontrado recogiendo los frutos de los árboles. También nos hacían saber sobre otras vidas que pasaban cerca en ese momento, ya fuese para nuestro cuidado y protección, o simplemente nos anunciaran que el ambiente se estaba ampliando con otras presencias. Estas son memorias recurrentes, a las que vuelvo cada vez que encuentro un obstáculo en mi camino. Allí es donde recupero fuerzas y desde donde vuelvo a empezar, con una mayor fuerza, que supera los obstáculos y da continuidad al recorrido.


También pulsan los recuerdos del amanecer en una casa construida con materiales del lugar, con parte del techo hecho de tejas de adobe crudo y otra parte de paja y madera. La parte de la casa construida con adobe y techo de tejas era la habitación en la que dormíamos. Como el clima tendía a ser más templado por la noche, este era el espacio adecuado para dormir.


La parte de la casa con paredes de barro y techo de paja, curiosamente, a pesar del riesgo de incendio, era el espacio de la cocina, precisamente porque la paja y el barro son térmicos. Ese espacio se calentaba menos durante el día y era donde se encendía la cocina a leña. La otra habitación, con techo de paja y paredes de palos secos, era donde se realizaban actividades colectivas como el telar, ya que el espacio donde se tejía necesitaba estar mejor ventilado. Nuestra arquitectura estaba adaptada a las actividades realizadas durante el día en cada uno de los espacios.


Foto: Alexia Melo


Cuando cumplí diez años, empecé a adiestrar bueyes. Fue así como aprendí que adiestrar y colonizar son lo mismo. Tanto el adiestrador como el colonizador comienzan por desterritorializar al ente atacado, quebrando su identidad, sacándolo de su cosmología, alejándolo de sus entes sagrados, imponiéndole nuevas formas de vida y dándole otro nombre. El proceso de denominación es un intento de borramiento de una memoria para que otra pueda crearse.


Hay adiestradores que pegan y adiestradores que dan cariño; hay adiestradores que castigan y adiestradores que dan comida para hacerlos adictos, pero todos son adiestradores. Y todo adiestramiento tiene el mismo propósito: hacer trabajar o producir objetos de disfrute y satisfacción. Sin embargo, no a todos los animales podemos adiestrarlos. Algunos quedan físicamente atrofiados, cuando se exige del animal un esfuerzo físico más allá de lo que es capaz. Otros quedan atrofiados mentalmente, cuando el animal sufre un shock mental violento.


De manera análoga, hay personas atrofiadas: personas que no fueron adiestradas para trabajar, pero que tampoco son pillas. Personas adiestradas para no tener un imaginario, para no lograr practicar su autogestión. Personas que no aprendieron a hacer nada ni aprendieron a extraer algo de lo ya hecho. Personas atrofiadas que deambulan sin saber adónde ir. O incluso, personas que fueron adiestradas y terminaron transformadas en población trabajadora fluctuante, que pasa una temporada en el sur o en el sudeste, en una servidumbre asalariada, y luego regresan.


Al dominar la técnica del adiestramiento, rápidamente me di cuenta de que, para enfrentarnos a la sociedad colonialista, a veces “necesitamos transformar las armas de nuestros enemigos en defensa”, como decía uno de mis grandes maestros de defensa. Entonces, para transformar el arte de denominar en un arte de defensa, resolvimos denominar nosotros también.

author: Rizomatica
title: Comunicado de amigos, familiares, lov y comunidades de los Presos Políticos Mapuche de Caso Grollmus de la Franja Lavkenche
content:
«COMUNICADO PÚBLICO


Lavken mapu, Pukem 2026.


Mari mari kom pu che, pu ke lov, pu ke mapu, eymun kom!

Tras reunirnos en txawün el día de hoy queremos dirigirinos a nuestro pueblo, a la opinión pública nacional e internacional, a la ocupación chilena en nuestro territorio.

19 de nuestros hermanos, compañeros, padre e hijos se encuentra ad portas de terminar su juicio oral, imputados todos por su supuesta participación en el atentado al Molino Grollmus. Lo vamos a decir de forma clara y sin metáforas, nuestros presos políticos son víctimas de la necesidad ansiosa del ministerio público por dar resultados al sistema político y a los colonos que ocupan nuestro territorio. Ellos no estan presos por ser delincuentes, sino, porque la unica forma que ha encontrado la ocupación para detener la justa y legitima lucha por el territorio y autonomía de los mapuche ha sido la persecución, los allanamientos, los desalojos, la prisión. Nuestros presos se encuentran en esa condición pues todos ellos se organizaron a lo largo y ancho de nuestro territorio para luchar por la recuperación de sus tierras, por levantar sus ngillatun, por dar dignidad a su gente.

El fiscal de la causa se encuentra con una querella en su contra por prevaricacion, los colonos Grollmus se juntaron directamente con el presidente Jose Kast, y el Ministro Arrau a definido públicamente este juicio como «trascendental para Chile». Durante el transcurso de las audiencias ha quedado en plena evidencia que el unico insumo de fiscalia es la declaración de personas sin nombre y rostro, nada más.

La situación es clara, nuestros hermanos, dignos y perseguidos, arriegan cadena perpetua solo por la inmesa presión del poder político para su encarcelamiento.

Hoy son los alegatos de clausura y declaramos que nuestros esfuerzos seran inclaudicables en búsqueda de justicia.


Amigos, familiares, lov y comunidades de los Presos Políticos Mapuche de Caso Grollmus de la Franja Lavkenche.»

Radio Kurruf

author: anred
title: Organizaciones populares repudian la privatización de Aysa frente al Ministerio de Economía
content:
Hoy, pese a la lluvia, representantes de organizaciones sociales, ambientales, vecinales, sindicatos y partidos se presentaron ante el Ministerio de Economía de la Nación para hacer entrega de una carta dirigida al ministro de Economía, Luis Andrés Caputo, expresando su rechazo al proceso de privatización de Agua y Saneamientos Argentinos (AySA).

Por Patricia Rodríguez para ANRed


En la presentación expusieron su rechazo al proceso de privatización. Empezando por la modificación del Marco Regulatorio (Dec. 493/25) que suprimió el Derecho Humano al Agua para habilitar los cortes del servicio en caso de dificultades de pago y bajo los estándares de control de calidad del agua, con los posibles impactos en la salud que esto puede significar. La privatización de AySA pone en discusión el futuro de un servicio esencial para millones de personas y puede tener consecuencias directas sobre las tarifas, la expansión de la infraestructura, el mantenimiento de las redes, los mecanismos de control y la calidad del agua y el saneamiento.


La carta presentada denuncia que se pretende volver a convertir el agua en una mercancía. La nefasta experiencia de la privatización de los años 90, significó tarifas dolarizadas impagables, incumplimiento reiterado de metas de expansión del servicio, creciente endeudamiento para fugar capitales, todos hechos que padecimos como pueblo en nuestros territorios. Esa experiencia privatizadora fracasada no puede volver a ocurrir.


Hoy en el nuevo contrato de concesión previsto para la empresa se le asegura rentas extraordinarias al futuro operador y cero riesgo empresario, al calcular una tasa de ganancia de la empresa en dólares. «Denunciamos que los usuarios deberán pagar una renta anual en dólares del 8,9% sobre la operación y expansión del servicio» expresaron.


Asimismo denuncian que el proceso de licitación en curso mantiene un secretismo injustificado ni siquiera el Ente Regulador conoce los contenidos exigidos en los pliegos de licitación. Esto atenta contra todo principio de transparencia y rendición de cuentas de la Administración Pública.


Reclamaron al gobierno que cumpla con la cautelar dictada en el juzgado de Primera Instancia en los Contencioso Administrativo N° 2 de La Plata, que suspendió el proceso de privatización, obligando al Ejecutivo Nacional a que abstenerse de modificar los parámetros de control de calidad de agua, reducción de exigencias regulatorias y postergación de planes de obras críticas. Debe suspenderse el proceso de privatización y se deben reactivar las obras públicas de saneamiento.


«Le informamos al Ministerio de Economía que no vamos a aceptar un nuevo saqueo y que los responsables de esta entrega son pasibles de ser juzgados por fraude en perjuicio de la Administración Pública» afirmaron.


Agregaron «desde nuestros espacios entendemos que el retraso en la apertura de los pliegos constituye, en este contexto, una oportunidad. Este tiempo adicional nos permite profundizar el trabajo conjunto, articular con nuevas organizaciones y sectores y unir las distintas luchas que se vienen desarrollando en defensa del agua, el ambiente, la salud, el trabajo y los servicios públicos».


En la asamblea las organizaciones consideraron urgente fortalecer la organización y ampliar la participación para masificar el repudio a la entrega del patrimonio nacional.


«La experiencia de nuestro territorio demuestra que los avances en materia de agua y saneamiento fueron posibles gracias a años de organización, lucha vecinal, trabajo comunitario y participación de distintos sectores. Por eso entendemos que, frente al actual proceso de privatización, la construcción de una respuesta colectiva resulta fundamental» recordaron.


Entre las organizaciones presentes estuvieron:

author: Gustavo Faleiros
title: Lula e Flávio falham ao unir meio ambiente e soberania em programas de governo
content:
Quer receber os textos desta coluna em primeira mão no seu e-mail? Assine a newsletter Ligando os pontos, enviada toda quinta-feira. Para receber as próximas edições,

inscreva-se aqui

.


Reconheço que me aproximei dos programas de governo dos dois principais candidatos à Presidência com a suspeita de que não encontraria muitos elementos para o debate ambiental. Normalmente, a manchete que cravamos a cada eleição presidencial é: “candidatos não incluem a questão ambiental entre suas prioridades”. Pois desta vez me enganei. Me meti ali nas páginas dos programas de governo de Lula e Flávio e encontrei referências frequentes aos temas mais importantes nesta área.


A transição ecológica, as cidades verdes, a adaptação às mudanças climáticas, o combate à mineração ilegal e o saneamento contextualizam ou são parte das propostas dos dois candidatos mais bem posicionados na disputa à Presidência.


Esta profusão de palavras-chave, entretanto, não diminui a percepção de que, qualquer que seja o vencedor, muitas das promessas ficarão no papel. A desconfiança é ainda maior: o próximo governo pode dobrar a aposta em um modelo de crescimento econômico contrário à sustentabilidade. Ou seja, priorizará grandes obras de infraestrutura com débeis processos de licenciamento ambiental e consulta aos povos afetados. Continuará uma corrida desenfreada por minério, petróleo e terra.


Ao ler os dois programas, me surpreendi ao ver que promessas de cuidado ao meio ambiente e de uso dos recursos naturais são tratadas como um tema de soberania. Quando os candidatos abordam setores estratégicos, como as terras raras, o consumo de energia, a infraestrutura digital e o agronegócio, a bandeira é a defesa das nossas riquezas contra interesses externos. Quais? Não fica claro.


Talvez faça sentido que seja assim, já que vivemos num mundo em que as relações comerciais estão abaladas pelas guerras reais e tarifárias. Todos estamos sofrendo as consequências, seja no preço dos combustíveis ou dos alimentos. Porém, me parece falacioso insinuar o nacionalismo nesta discussão, já que o país não poderá prescindir do mercado externo para obter crescimento econômico. Somos uma nação prioritariamente exportadora de

commodities

 agrícolas e minerais.


Ao fazer de seu primeiro evento de campanha a promoção da exploração de petróleo na Foz do Amazonas, o presidente acabou por desacreditar aquilo que está colocado em seu programa. Sim, a Petrobras está à frente da exploração na margem equatorial, mas está ali de mãozinha dada com a americana ExxonMobil, a maior petroleira do mundo.


Não acho que a solução seja o caminho chavista da Venezuela – nacionalização completa da produção de petróleo. Mas explorar combustíveis fósseis nesta altura do campeonato, quando deveríamos estar reduzindo as emissões de carbono, é um caminho bem diferente do proposto no documento de campanha, que garante que estamos em plena transição ecológica.


Ainda no programa de Lula, o argumento sobre uma nova industrialização, com incentivos fiscais para a economia verde, fica bastante frágil diante dos atropelos que estão ocorrendo no licenciamento de grandes obras e projetos. Apesar de publicamente criticar a nova lei de licenciamento ambiental, o governo editou o

Decreto 12.673 em outubro de 2025

author: A.N.A.
title: Sou a Anarquia!!!
content:
Nasci com a primeira revolta insubmissa, inquieta, desgrenhada. Construí a mim mesma desnuda, bela, irreverente. Desde meus ossos inermes partiu a primeira blasfêmia ao criador… Neguei-me a ser submetida, dirigida, apadrinhada. Transformei-me em apóstata, fui acusada de irreligiosidade. Fui condenada, mas minhas asas eram de fênix, e rapidamente abandonei as fogueiras e atravessei os oceanos… Vi jugos em todo lugar, dores e fome, discursos e lamentos, aprendi o desespero. Cavei com as unhas uma trincheira de sonhos e me embriaguei com esse bando de jovens loucos, poetas náufragos de volta à Espanha de trinta e seis… Olhei à esquerda, olhei à direita e vi rostos sujos escondidos atrás de limpos uniformes vertendo o sangue dos povos em nome da justiça, da dialética e outras quintessências enjoativas… E peguei a raiva e afiei-a e lancei raios contra os tronos, inimiga dos governos, inimiga das pátrias, inimiga da dor. Abraço o mundo, vivo e não imploro, amo e resisto suas tiranias.


Sou a Anarquia!!!


(Anônimo)
